author: Hermas
addressee: The Church, especially its leaders, and all the saints/elect of God
occasion: Hermas, a former slave and businessman, receives visions, commandments, and parables from an angelic shepherd to call the Church to repentance. The text states that repentance has a fixed end for the saints, but continues for the nations until the last day.
argument: Hermas is shown that his own sins and his family's sins have brought him under God's anger, but God in his mercy offers a chance for repentance. The Church appears as an old woman who grows younger in three successive visions, representing the spiritual renewal of Hermas and the community through revelation and repentance. The Shepherd, an angel of repentance, then gives Hermas twelve commandments that teach purity, truth, patience, and single-minded faith, and a series of parables that illustrate how the rich and poor, the repentant and the unrepentant, will be treated. The work concludes with a vision of the tower's completion, where only those who have received the name of the Son of God and been clothed with the virtues of the virgins will enter the kingdom.

outline.move: Hermas sees his former mistress Rhoda in a vision and is rebuked for his lustful thoughts; an old woman (the Church) appears and tells him to repent and correct his household.
The old woman gives Hermas a little book to copy; its contents are revealed, calling his family and the church leaders to repentance and warning of a coming great tribulation.
The old woman shows Hermas a vision of a tower being built on water, explains the meaning of its stones and the seven women (virtues) supporting it, and urges the rich to share with the poor.
Hermas sees a great beast, a type of the coming tribulation, and escapes it through faith; the Church, now as a bride, explains the beast's four colors.
The Shepherd, an angel of repentance, appears to Hermas and commissions him to write down the commandments and parables.
Commandment 1: Believe in one God, fear him, and practice self-control.
Commandment 2: Be simple and innocent; avoid slander and give generously to all in need.
Commandment 3: Love truth and speak no lie, for lying grieves the Holy Spirit.

Commandment 4: Keep purity in thought and marriage; a husband should remain by himself if his wife is unrepentant in adultery, and if he marries another he commits adultery. The text states that current and future believers have no repentance for sins, only forgiveness of prior sins.
Commandment 5: Be patient and understanding; anger and bitterness drive away the Holy Spirit.
Commandment 6: Two angels, one of righteousness and one of wickedness, influence every person; learn to distinguish their works.
Commandment 7: Fear the Lord and keep his commandments, but do not fear the devil, who has no power.
Commandment 8: Practice self-control from evil deeds but do not refrain from good deeds; lists of vices to avoid and virtues to pursue.
Commandment 9: Remove double-mindedness; ask God for what you need without doubting, and you will receive it.
Commandment 10: Remove grief and put on cheerfulness, for grief grieves the Holy Spirit and makes prayer ineffective.
Commandment 11: Test prophets by their lives; true prophets are humble and speak only when God wills, false prophets are greedy and flatter the double-minded.
Commandment 12: Put away evil desire and put on good desire; the devil can wrestle but cannot overcome those who resist him.
Parable 1: Christians are resident aliens in this world; they should invest in the needy, not in earthly property.
Parable 2: The elm and the vine illustrate how the rich and the poor help each other: the poor man's prayer gives power to the rich man's alms.
Parable 3: In this world, the righteous and sinners look alike, like trees in winter.
Parable 4: In the age to come, the righteous will be revealed as fruitful trees in summer, while sinners will be burned.
Parable 5: True fasting is keeping God's commandments; the parable of the vineyard and the faithful servant shows that extra good works bring greater honor.

Parable 6: Three shepherds appear: an angel of luxury and deceit, an angel of punishment who takes sheep from the first, and the interpreting Shepherd. The indulgent are punished in proportion to their sins to bring them to repentance.
The Shepherd explains that Hermas's household sins have brought the angel of punishment upon him, and he must endure affliction so his family may repent.

Parable 8: A great willow tree (the Law of God, which is the Son of God proclaimed to the ends of the earth) gives rods to the people; the rods are planted and many revive, showing that repentance can restore many, though some with dry rods are permanently rejected.

Parable 9: A great tower is built on a rock and a gate (the Son of God) with stones from twelve mountains (the nations); the virgins (virtues) carry the stones through the gate, and the Lord of the tower tests and replaces the faulty stones.
The angel who first delivered Hermas to the Shepherd returns, commends him, and charges him to continue his ministry, with the virgins as his helpers.

cast.name: Hermas
cast.who: The narrator and visionary, a former slave and businessman, now a prophet of repentance.

cast.name: Rhoda
cast.who: Hermas's former mistress, whom he sees in a vision and is rebuked for lusting after.

cast.name: The Church
cast.who: An old woman who appears in visions, growing younger as repentance progresses; she is the pre-existent Church.

cast.name: The Shepherd
cast.who: The angel of repentance, sent to dwell with Hermas and teach him the commandments and parables.

cast.name: The Angel of Punishment
cast.who: A righteous angel who punishes those who stray from God, to bring them to repentance.

cast.name: The Angel of Luxury and Deceit
cast.who: A young shepherd who leads people astray with pleasures and false delights.

cast.name: Michael
cast.who: The great and glorious angel who has authority over God's people and gives the Law into the hearts of believers.

cast.name: Clement
cast.who: A church leader in Rome to whom Hermas is to send a copy of the book for distribution to other cities.

cast.name: Grapte
cast.who: A woman in Rome who is to instruct the widows and orphans.

cast.name: Maximus
cast.who: A church leader warned of coming tribulation and the danger of denying the faith.

key_terms.sense: Repentance, the central theme: a turning of the whole heart to God, with a limited opportunity for those already called
Double-mindedness, wavering between faith and doubt, a daughter of the devil
The tower being built, representing the Church, built of stones (the faithful) on a rock (the Son of God)
The Church, pre-existent and created first, appearing as an old woman and as a tower
Self-control, especially from evil desires, a daughter of Faith
Patience, long-suffering, in which the Lord dwells
Anger, quick temper, a bitter spirit that drives away the Holy Spirit
The seal, the name of the Son of God received in baptism
The Son of God, the rock and gate of the tower, through whom alone one enters the kingdom
The angel of repentance, the Shepherd himself, given authority over repentance
Tribulation, the coming great affliction, a type of which is the beast
The virgins, holy spirits or virtues (Faith, Self-control, etc.) who carry the stones into the tower
The elect, God's chosen people, the faithful
The double-minded, those who waver in faith and are easily led astray

scripture: The author uses the Septuagint (LXX) and refers to the apocryphal book of Eldad and Modat. Psalm numbering follows the LXX.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within the 2nd century CE.
The precise identity of the 'angel of luxury and deceit' beyond the text's description.
Whether the 'twelve mountains' correspond to specific historical nations or are purely symbolic.
The exact relationship between the Shepherd and the 'glorious angel' who sent him.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The text states that repentance has a fixed end for the saints, but continues for the nations until the last day.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὤμοσεν γὰρ ὁ δεσπότης κατὰ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς αὐτοῦ: ἐὰν ὡρισμένης τῆς ἡμέρας ταύτης ἔτι ἁμάρτησις γένηται, μὴ ἔχειν αὐτοὺς σωτηρίαν: ἡ γὰρ μετάνοια τοῖς δικαίοις ἔχει τέλος: πεπλήρωνται αἱ ἡμέραι μετανοίας πᾶσιν τοῖς ἁγίοις: καὶ τοῖς δὲ ἔθνεσιν μετάνοιά ἐστιν ἕως ἐσχάτης ἡμέρας.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text states that for the righteous/saints, repentance has an end (τέλος) and the days of repentance are fulfilled, but for the nations repentance exists until the last day. However, this is specifically about a fixed day that has been appointed, after which sin will no longer be forgiven for the elect, not a general statement about all future time.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Church appears as an old woman who grows younger in three successive visions, representing the spiritual renewal of Hermas and the community through revelation and repentance.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τῇ μὲν πρώτῃ ὁράσει τῇ περυσινῇ λίαν πρεσβυτέρα καὶ ἐν καθέδρᾳ καθημένη... τῇ δὲ ἑτέρᾳ ὁράσει τὴν μὲν ὄψιν νεωτέραν εἶχεν... τῇ δὲ τρίτῃ ὁράσει ὅλη νεωτέρα καὶ κάλλει ἐκπρεπεστάτη
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Church appears in three forms with changing age, but the interpretation given in the text is specifically about the condition of the spirits of the people: first old because of their weakness and double-mindedness, then younger when renewed by the revelation, then fully young and beautiful when they received the good news. It represents the spiritual renewal of the community, but the text explicitly ties it to their spiritual condition, not just 'revelation and repentance' generally.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The text states that current and future believers have no repentance for sins, only forgiveness of prior sins.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ νῦν πιστεύσαντες ἢ μέλλοντες πιστεύειν μετάνοιαν ἁμαρτιῶν οὐκ ἔχουσιν, ἄφεσιν δὲ ἔχουσι τῶν προτέρων ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν... τοῖς οὖν κληθεῖσι πρὸ τούτων τῶν ἡμερῶν ἔθηκεν ὁ κύριος μετάνοιαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text states that those who now believe or will believe 'have no repentance of sins' (μετανόιαν ἁμαρτιῶν οὐκ ἔχουσιν) but have forgiveness of prior sins. However, it immediately clarifies that the Lord established repentance for those called BEFORE these days, and that if someone sins after this great and holy calling, they have ONE repentance. The claim oversimplifies by saying 'no repentance'—the text actually allows one repentance after baptism for those who are tempted by the devil, but warns that repeated sin after this is 'unprofitable' and such a person will 'with difficulty live.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Section 9 covers Commandment 4: Keep purity in thought and marriage; a husband should remain by himself if his wife is unrepentant in adultery, and if he marries another he commits adultery.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀπολυσάτω, φησίν, αὐτὴν καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ ἐφ̓ ἑαυτῷ μενέτω: ἐὰν δὲ ἀπολύσας τὴν γυναῖκα ἑτέραν γαμήσῃ, καὶ αὐτὸς μοιχᾶται... ἀλλὰ δεῖ παραδεχθῆναι τὸν ἡμαρτηκότα καὶ μετανοοῦντα, μὴ ἐπὶ πολὺ δέ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The commandment does say the husband should remain by himself and that if he marries another he commits adultery. However, it also states that if the wife repents, the husband MUST receive her back—'he sins and brings great sin upon himself' if he does not receive her. The outline omits this crucial requirement of receiving the repentant wife, and also omits that the husband should not marry another because 'for the servants of God there is one repentance.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Section 22 covers Parable 5: True fasting is keeping God's commandments; the parable of the vineyard and the faithful servant shows that extra good works bring greater honor.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐὰν δέ τι ἀγαθὸν ποιήσῃς ἐκτὸς τῆς ἐντολῆς τοῦ θεοῦ, σεαυτῷ περιποιήσῃ δόξαν περισσοτέραν καὶ ἔσῃ ἐνδοξότερος παρὰ τῷ θεῷ οὗ ἔμελλες εἶναι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The parable does mention that doing good beyond the commandment brings greater glory. However, the main point of the parable is about fasting properly—abstaining from evil, serving God with a pure heart, keeping commandments, and giving to the poor what one would have spent on food. The 'extra good works' framing understates the central teaching about fasting as ethical living and almsgiving.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Section 25 covers Parable 8: A great willow tree (the Law of God, which is the Son of God proclaimed to the ends of the earth) gives rods to the people
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ δένδρον τοῦτο τὸ μέγα τὸ σκεπάζον πεδία καὶ ὄρη καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν νόμος θεοῦ ἐστιν ὁ δοθεὶς εἰς ὅλον τὸν κόσμον: ὁ δὲ νόμος οὗτος υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐστι κηρυχθεὶς εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς γῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: The willow tree is identified as 'the Law of God given into the whole world,' and 'this Law is the Son of God proclaimed to the ends of the earth.' However, the brief incorrectly calls this 'Parable 8' when it is actually Parable 8 in the sequence but the text itself doesn't number them this way consistently. More importantly, the brief's parenthetical is slightly garbled: the Law IS the Son of God proclaimed, not 'which is the Son of God proclaimed'—it's an identification, not a relative clause.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Michael: The great and glorious angel who has authority over God's people and gives the Law into the hearts of believers.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ ἄγγελος ὁ μέγας καὶ ἔνδοξος Μιχαὴλ ὁ ἔχων τὴν ἐξουσίαν τούτου τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ διακυβερνῶν αὐτούς: οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ διδοὺς αὐτοῖς τὸν νόμον εἰς τὰς καρδίας τῶν πιστευόντων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says Michael 'has the authority over this people and governs them' and 'gives them the Law into the hearts of the believers.' However, the text does NOT say he gives the Law 'into the hearts of believers'—it says he gives the Law 'into the hearts of those who believe' (τῶν πιστευόντων), which is slightly different. More importantly, the brief omits that Michael is specifically identified as the one who 'visits them to see if they have kept it.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Angel (who delivered Hermas to the Shepherd): Introduced with 'λέγει μοι' or 'φησίν', sections: ['27']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ποστ#3υαμ περσξριπσεραμ λιβρυμ ηυνξ, ϝενιτ νυντιυς ιλλε, #3υι με τραδιδερατ ηυιξ παστορι... ετ αδστιτιτ αδ δεχτεραμ ηιξ παστορ. δεινδε ϝοξαϝιτ με ετ ηαεξ μιηι διχιτ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The angel is introduced as 'nuntius ille, qui me tradiderat huic pastori' (that messenger who had delivered me to this shepherd). He speaks to Hermas, but the brief's claim about 'λέγει μοι' or 'φησίν' is not verifiable from the garbled Latin/Greek text of section 27, which is heavily corrupted. The brief should note the textual corruption in this section.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Ἐλδὰδ καὶ Μωδάτ: Eldad and Modat
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς γέγραπται ἐν τῷ Ἐλδὰδ καὶ Μωδάτ, τοῖς προφητεύσασιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ τῷ λαῷ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text mentions 'Eldad and Modat' as prophets who prophesied in the wilderness to the people, but this is actually a reference to Eldad and Medad (from Numbers 11:26-29). The name is 'Μωδάτ' in the manuscript, but this is a known variant. The brief correctly identifies the reference but should note this is an apocryphal/prophetic reference, not a canonical book.
